title: Does Tokyo need self-driving taxis? Waymo thinks so, plans to launch fleet soon
description: It’s hard to see why Tokyoites would prefer self-driving cabs to regular ones, but that might not be what Waymo is betting on. Japan has, by and large, passed on ride-sharing services. Though they’ve flourished in many other parts of the world, Japan’s demographics and public transportation infrastructure is such that owning your own car […]
content:
It’s hard to see why Tokyoites would prefer self-driving cabs to regular ones, but that might not be what Waymo is betting on.

Japan has, by and large, passed on ride-sharing services. Though they’ve flourished in many other parts of the world, Japan’s demographics and public transportation infrastructure is such that owning your own car is a discretionary luxury in urban and suburban communities, and so car-owners usually aren’t in income brackets where they have a strong incentive or need to make a few extra bucks as drivers. Meanwhile, there’s not much passenger demand among residents of rural Japan, where having a car of your own is pretty much a necessity on a daily basis.

The result is that Uber’s presence in Japan is far larger in the food delivery business than the people moving one. However, even if the country is largely skipping ride-sharing, Waymo still thinks it has a chance to shake up the Japanese taxi industry, and it’s looking to introduce fully self-driving cabs in Tokyo soon.

Last year, the U.S.-based Waymo entered into a strategic partnership with Japanese taxi operator Nihon Kotsu and Go, a Japanese taxi-hailing app partly owned by Nihon Kotsu. In the year since, they’ve been conducting tests of Waymo vehicles on Tokyo streets, with a Nihon Kotsu driver onboard to ensure safety and take over when needed. The three companies now feel they’re ready to start taking steps towards the next phase of their plan, launching Japan’s first fleet of fully self-driving, unmanned taxis, which they hope to have running about Tokyo’s streets sometime in 2027.

The companies say that safety will be their highest priority as they gradually introduce a growing number of self-driving taxis, with an initial goal of approximately 100 vehicles in Tokyo. Tokyo’s road network is a complex mixture of congested major thoroughfares and narrow backstreets, with a very large percentage of uncontrolled or irregularly shaped intersections, all of which make self-driving a challenge from a technical standpoint.

▼ There’s no word as to whether or not Waymo’s self-driving cars will follow the Japanese taxi norm of lace doilies on the seats.

Even if Waymo’s vehicles can learn to navigate Tokyo’s streets, though, there’s still the question of how much consumer demand there is in the city for self-driving taxis. Ostensibly, eliminating the driver would allow for lower operating costs, which could, theoretically, be passed on to consumers in the form of lower fares. However, because Tokyo  has such convenient train, subway, and bus networks, taxi travel is already seen as something of a luxury among locals and travelers. Most people who are looking for a cab aren’t particularly concerned about the price, and Waymo would probably have to offer fares that are substantially cheaper than conventional taxis’ in order to entice rail or bus users strongly enough to take a ride in their self-driving cars.

The added pickup convenience presented by self-driving cabs might also not have such significant appeal, since taxi usage in Tokyo tends to be either between two downtown locations or, if the trains have already stopped running for the night, from downtown back to the suburbs. In either case, the rides are starting in a developed location, where it’s usually not hard to find a taxi on the street. By comparison, calling a taxi to come pick you up at your home in the suburbs is a far less common scenario.

All that said, it is true that Japan’s professional driver workforce, including taxi drivers, has been steadily growing older, with fewer new drivers coming into the industry than veteran drivers retiring. As such, Waymo and Nihon Kotsu might not be looking to launch driverless taxis because they think customers will prefer them to conventional cabs, but as preparation for an expected coming labor shortage that could make it difficult to find and hire enough human drivers. If/when that happens, there’s bound to be a portion of the population that still feels uneasy riding in a self-driving car, but if they have to, they’d probably rather ride in one from a provider that isn’t a complete newcomer to the market, so Waymo’s starting fleet in Tokyo is probably more about trying to build trust and recognition than making a quick profit.

title: Snow Salt Soft Cream Cafe & Bar for grown-ups opens in Tokyo’s Ueno area with a bookish surprise
description: Adults can indulge in a coffee or alcoholic beverage paired with soft serve ice cream at this new oasis of calm in the city. Snow Salt Soft Cream Cafe & Bar is a new soft serve ice cream brand from the Hokkaido-based company Daruma that’s said to use an exquisite blend of milk and salt […]
content:
Adults can indulge in a coffee or alcoholic beverage paired with soft serve ice cream at this new oasis of calm in the city.

Snow Salt Soft Cream Cafe & Bar is a new soft serve ice cream brand from the Hokkaido-based company Daruma that’s said to use an exquisite blend of milk and salt in its base. The shop is only a five-minute walk from the Hirokoji Exit of JR Ueno Station in a quiet neighborhood that’s in the exact opposite direction of the noisy Ameyoko shopping street.

Never ones to resist a sweet treat for grown-ups, we set our sights on checking it out as soon as we could. We ended up visiting on a weekday less than a week after its grand opening, and lovely celebratory bouquets of orchids and other flowers still graced its entrance.

The soft serve utilizes milk from Hokkaido’s Iwase Farm and salt sourced from Okinawa–two ingredients from extreme ends of the country. The heart of the food menu centers on soft serve dishes, including the standard “Snow Salt” soft serve, “Snow on Snow” soft serve combo with chunks of milk bread, espresso affogato, Hokkaido yogurt affogato, and whiskey affogato. Beverages include coffee or espresso-based drinks as well as ones with alcohol such as highballs.

After ordering, we took a moment to look around. While we initially thought that the shop emphasized takeout, upon closer inspection, we soon realized that there was a third-floor Picture Book Lounge where customers could sit down and eat. The space is perfect for people wanting to take a quiet moment for themselves while flipping through the pages of a nostalgic childhood tale.

After a short wait, our order of iced coffee (480 yen [US$3.15]) and espresso affogato (780 yen) arrived. We had debated getting the coffee when we were already getting espresso along with the dessert, but our craving for it won us over. Oh well–it’s not like our office isn’t familiar with overly caffeinated writers who get up to weird antics…

We resolved to first try a bite of the famous Snow Salt soft serve with nothing else added.

The soft serve’s milk flavor was rich and full-bodied with a decent weight to it, despite it melting easily in our mouths. The hint of added salt also balanced out the sweetness perfectly.

OK, now it was time to make the affogato. We drizzled some espresso on top and watched as the hot liquid forged small rivers in the soft serve.

The dish had an amazing synergy. The espresso naturally added bitterness to the flavor, which in turn actually caused the sweetness to stand out more, but not at the loss of the former. We imagine that the whiskey affogato would result in a similarly delicious effect.

While the hustle and bustle of other parts of Ueno are undoubtedly fun, Snow Salt creates a quiet, relaxing space for you to pair an adult snack with a nostalgic picture book. Daruma’s Tokyo Office is also located on the 4th floor of the same building, making the space into a family affair.

If your idea of sweets is something more along the line of Japanese-style pudding, you may be interested in finding your oasis at this cafe in another part of the city instead.

title: New Ranma 1/2 anime tableware and lifestyle goods are appropriately multi-faceted [Photos]
description: The Rumiko Takahashi anime remake inspires a line of items for cooking, carrying, or just admiring. The new Ranma 1/2 anime is a hit, finding fans among both newcomers to creator Rumiko Takahashi’s martial arts romantic comedy and veteran otaku who enjoyed the original TV series from the late ‘80s/early ‘90s. However, as is often […]
content:
The Rumiko Takahashi anime remake inspires a line of items for cooking, carrying, or just admiring.

The new Ranma 1/2 anime is a hit, finding fans among both newcomers to creator Rumiko Takahashi’s martial arts romantic comedy and veteran otaku who enjoyed the original TV series from the late ‘80s/early ‘90s. However, as is often the norm with modern anime series, the Ranma 1/2 remake takes breaks between its seasons. Thankfully, these haven’t been too long, with Seasons 1 and 2 airing in the fall of 2024 and 2025, respectively, and that pace is set to continue with Season 3 scheduled to start in October.

But if you need a dose of Ranma fun even sooner, there’s a new line of clever tableware and lifestyle goods releasing this month.

The motif for many of the designs comes from the in-anime Cat Cafe/Nekohanten, a Chinese restaurant run by the grandmother of character Shampoo, one of protagonist Ranma’s many unasked-for fiancés.

The lineup, offered by Japanese clothing and homewares brand Studio Clip, includes stoneware ceramic Cat Cafe ramen bowls and spoons, decorated with illustrations of several members of the cast.

▼ The bowl is microwave and dishwasher-safe.

▼ The kanji for “cat” appears at the tip of the spoon’s handle.

While they’re functional, you could make the argument that these items are just too pretty to cook and eat with. Luckily, they all work great as decorative items too, and the two-tiered bamboo steamer could actually work quite well as a unique organizer for small items.

There are items specifically designed for storage and carrying, though, from lightweight eco shopping bags to embroidered cotton and satin totes. One of the eco bags even folds up to fit inside a female Ranma plushie, which can also be used as a bag strap charm.

Getting back to the drinkware, there’s a ceramic tea service as well as a glass tea-strainer mug.

The cleverest designs of all, though, are the insulated bag modeled after the Cat Cafe’s metallic carrier box for delivery orders…

…and the oven mitt shaped like P-chan, one of the series’ many cute animals who’s actually the transformed state of a cursed martial artist.

Out of the items shown here, the eco bag with plushie is the priciest, at 4,400 yen (US$28), with the rest mostly in the 2,000-3,000-yen range. The whole line is available as of September 18 through Studio Clip’s online store (here) and physical shops.

title: Tokyo to repaint streets over rule that makes it impossible for cars to pass bicycles
description: Some rules are meant to be broken. A few months back, Japan made some sweeping changes to bicycle laws, introducing the notorious “blue tickets” for infractions such as riding too fast on a sidewalk, riding with an umbrella, or riding while using a smartphone. The laws came into effect along with a fairly large crackdown […]
content:
Some rules are meant to be broken.

A few months back, Japan made some sweeping changes to bicycle laws, introducing the notorious “blue tickets” for infractions such as riding too fast on a sidewalk, riding with an umbrella, or riding while using a smartphone. The laws came into effect along with a fairly large crackdown on such behavior by police departments across the country.

And for a while it worked. People by and large traded in their umbrellas for raincoats. However, once the full force of the summer sun kicked in and after a few torrential rainstorms, many people decided to hell with it and started using umbrellas again. The problem with that is these same cyclists are still adhering to the no-sidewalk rule, which means drivers now have to put up with these slow-moving vehicles that are sometimes up to over a meter wide. 

Quite a few roads do have bicycle lanes to accommodate this, but they’re pretty absurd in practice. Cars and trucks often park right in them, mopeds frequently make them their own personal passing lane, and the bike lanes often just don’t fit. Especially in major cities, there are a lot of roads that are literally ancient and can’t be expanded due to the dense buildings along them.

▼ An all-too-common scene: A cyclist going around a car parked in the bike lane while another car goes extra wide to overtake the bicycle at the same time.

To make matters worse, traffic rules dictate that cars must give at least one meter (three feet) of distance when passing a bike. At the same time, if the road has a yellow center line, then you must never cross over it, so there are many instances where a car might be legally unable to pass a bicycle. You’re technically not even allowed to honk your horn at them to move over, because that is also a violation known as “abuse of the horn.”

Of course, in reality, when faced with this situation, most cars would just go over the yellow line to pass anyway. I’d also like to think that any cop would consider that to be the most reasonable course of action and let it slide despite it being a violation. I actually learned firsthand from taking a driving test with the police that crossing the yellow line was tolerated to a certain degree rather than an automatic failure.

Still, that’s a worry normal drivers are best left without, and there’s really no point in having paradoxical traffic rules in the first place. So, the Tokyo Metropolitan Police announced they will repaint about 1,700 kilometers (1,056 miles) of yellow lines white. Unlike yellow lines, it is permitted to cross over white lines in cases such as overtaking bicycles. Tokyo’s Nakano Ward is even going as far as repainting all of its yellow lines white.

In online comments, readers of the news felt this was just another way the new blue ticket laws are spreading misery even beyond the cyclists they directly target.

“These rule changes are just screwing up everything.”
“Didn’t they consider this before making the new rules?”
“On a lot of narrow roads in Tokyo they just got rid of the line altogether.”
“Honestly, they should have just been stricter on the speeds of bikes on sidewalks. Some idiot said they should ride on the road, and now look at this mess.”
“It’s a broken system for anyone who follows the rules.”
“I’ve seen this so many times on the road since April. Even cop cars are doing it, lol.”
“Repainting them white? So why were they yellow in the first place?”
“The people drafting these laws don’t ride bikes or drive. They’re just chauffeured everywhere they go.”
“This will never get better until the infrastructure improves.”

It’s hard to blame the urban planners for this problem, as it’s an impossible situation to begin with. In order for cities like Tokyo to widen their roads, it would require tearing down literally thousands of buildings.

▼ This road currently being built has a nicely demarcated bicycle lane and space for everyone to enjoy. Unfortunately, it’s only about 500 meters long, required tearing down several blocks of shops and houses, and is basically a drop in the ocean.

▼ At the end of the finished construction, you can see the old road on the right, which is narrower than the new sidewalk.

With no practical solution in sight, motorists, cyclists, and pedestrians will just have to keep on winging it as we go. However you do move about in Japan, just be sure to do it safely, because many of the roads we share aren’t big enough for everyone.

Source: FNN Prime Online, Hachima Kiko

title: Japan’s new Pokémon Poké Ball hotel releases new details, and it’s giving away free stays [Video]
description: Some, but not all, of the secrets surrounding Japan’s awesome Poké Ball hotel have been revealed. At the start of the month Pokémon fans got some news that sounded too good to be true: there’s a new hotel opening in Japan where you can spend the night in Poké Balls! We’re not talking about a […]
content:
Some, but not all, of the secrets surrounding Japan’s awesome Poké Ball hotel have been revealed.

At the start of the month Pokémon fans got some news that sounded too good to be true: there’s a new hotel opening in Japan where you can spend the night in Poké Balls! We’re not talking about a regular hotel that’s slapping some Pokémon artwork on its walls, either, but actual Poké Ball-shaped structures big enough for people to sleep in.

Rest assured that the Poké Ball-Themed Hotel is real. However, the Pokémon Company and creative partner design firm Not a Hotel were coy as to where exactly fans will be resting, saying only that the hotel would be someplace in Hokkaido, Japan’s northernmost prefecture. They’ve now released a new batch of information, providing further details as to what guests can expect and revealing that the Poké Ball hotel will be located in the town of Tomakomai, about one hour south from Sapporo by train or car.

With their lakeside location and detached design, the Poké Balls function like unique camping cabins. A diameter of three meters (9.8 feet) means the interior dimensions are going to be cozy rather than palatial, but a soft, high-quality circular mattress ensures a good night’s sleep and comfy lounging, with a curved window allowing you to look out on the water and surrounding forest while still lying down.

The Poké Balls are designed to be big enough to accommodate two adult guests. Should you find yourself wanting even more companionship, by using the room’s tablet you can select a Pokémon to bid you good night when you turn off the lights, and good morning when you awake the next day.

The focus on restfulness comes from the fact that the Poké Ball-Themed Hotel is part of both the 30th anniversary celebration for the Pokémon franchise as a whole and also part of the 3rd anniversary festivities for wellness app/game Pokémon Sleep.

▼ New video preview for the Poké Ball-Themed Hotel

As you can probably tell from the above photos and video, the Poké Ball’s don’t have their own bathroom or shower. Instead, there’s a shared facility for such needs, though it too is stylish and classy, while also keeping to the theme with tiles in the colors of Snorlax. Likewise, as the Poké Balls have no dining area, meals are served in a cottage a five-minute walk away, where guests will also encounter sleeping Pokémon statues similar to the ones seen at the recent (and adorable) Pokémon Sleep event in Yokohama.

▼ The Snorlax-motif shower room and dining cottage interior can be seen at the point queued in this video.

There’s a bit of mystery remaining, though, in that the Poké Ball-Themed Hotel’s exact address still isn’t listed on its website. However, with Tomakomai having a number of campgrounds, including one called Arten Auto Resort Tomakomai that’s located near a lake, it’s likely that the Poké Ball-Themed Hotel’s Poké Balls are being installed in an existing camping area that’s serving as the facility manager/operator.

▼ In any case, Tomakomai isn’t all that large of a city, so even without a pinpoint location, folding a Poké Ball stay into your Hokkaido travel plans shouldn’t be too tricky, geographically speaking.

Also not yet revealed: pricing details. However, we do know that up to 20 lucky guests will be staying for free, thanks to a promotional campaign that’s giving away one night’s stay for 10 winners, each of whom are allowed to bring a traveling companion too. To enter, you’ll need to download the Pokémon Sleep app and follow its official Twitter account, then repost the following post using its embedded button and fill out the entry form.

【お知らせ】
「泊まれるモンスターボール」に抽選で10組様をご招待します。
大自然の中で特別な宿泊体験をお過ごしください！

①本アカウントをフォロー&アプリDL
②下のボタンからポスト
③専用フォーム入力で応募完了

応募者全員に「げんきマクラ&ポケサブレ」プレゼント

— 『Pokémon Sleep（ポケモンスリープ）』公式 (@PokemonSleepApp) September 15, 2026

There are three entry deadlines, September 17, 23, and 30, each corresponding to different dates on which winners are eligible to stay (October 8-10, October 10-14, and October 14-18, respectively). Regular reservations are yet to open, but when they do, what with Hokkaido’s heavy winter snows making it not the most pleasant place for quasi-camping in the winter, demand is sure to be high for fall stays.

Related: Poké Ball-Themed Hotel official website, Pokémon Sleep official Twitter account

title: Are Japanese temples on Mt Koya cashing in on the foreign tourism boom?
description: With more than 100 million yen in underreported income, questions are being raised over the morals of profiting from overseas tourists. A lot of businesses and organisations in Japan are seeking to make the most of the current boom in tourism by finding new ways to promote themselves and appeal to the foreign tourist market. […]
content:
With more than 100 million yen in underreported income, questions are being raised over the morals of profiting from overseas tourists.

A lot of businesses and organisations in Japan are seeking to make the most of the current boom in tourism by finding new ways to promote themselves and appeal to the foreign tourist market.

However, when that organisation is tied up with religion, it can blur the lines between what’s morally right and wrong, which is the situation that Japan’s world-famous religious site Mt Koya has now found itself in.

Located in the mountains of Wakayama Prefecture, Mt Koya has long been a revered religious site for pilgrims, and is so special it’s part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The site draws tourists from around the world, with many wanting to fully immerse themselves in the otherworldly spirit of the holy mountain by staying in temple accommodation, known as shukubo.

▼ Mt Koya, or “Koyasan” as it’s known in Japanese.

Following a recent tax investigation, it was found that religious corporations operating shukubo on Mt Koya had underreported more than 100 million yen (US$650,000) in income collectively, with around 90 million yen attributed to one temple, Sojiin. In this case, the family of the chief priest was found to have used income from the temple lodging for personal expenses over a three-year period. The tax authorities treated this as undeclared remuneration, and the religious corporation was hit with around 40 million yen in additional taxes and penalties.

The issue came to light on 10 September, when reports emerged that the Osaka Regional Taxation Bureau had investigated more than 10 religious corporations operating shukubo on Mt Koya, with more than half of those investigated found to have failed to properly declare income. The news was widely reported in Japan, putting the spotlight on how religious organisations are making money from the current tourism boom.

In terms of taxes, income from religious activities such as donations and offerings is generally exempt from taxation, while income earned through revenue-generating businesses such as accommodation is taxable. So although staying at a temple may be part of a spiritual or cultural experience, if that temple is operating accommodation as a business, the income it earns from those stays is subject to tax.

▼ Mt Koya is dotted with moss-covered religious sites and graves.

There’s certainly plenty of money being made from tourist stays. Mt Koya has 117 temples, 51 of which operate shukubo, and in 2025 around 117,500 foreign guests stayed overnight on the mountain, a 10-percent increase from the previous year. Shukubo, which traditionally provided accommodation for monks and pilgrims, have become increasingly popular with tourists from overseas, offering experiences such as Buddhist vegetarian meals, morning services, meditation and sutra copying.

As the number of foreign visitors has increased, so too has the price of temple stays, with some rooms on Mt Koya now costing more than 150,000 yen for two adults per night. According to one visitor, the same temple charging those prices now was only charging roughly 20,000 to 30,000 yen per person just four years ago.

The Koyasan Shukubo Association says that around 40 years ago, a one-night stay with two meals cost about 7,000 yen. Since the pandemic, government subsidies helped some lodgings upgrade their facilities, contributing to what the association describes as a move towards more luxurious accommodation. Today, some shukubo can offer rooms and facilities that look more like those of a luxury ryokan than the humble temple lodgings used by visitors in the past.

▼ Many of the temples on Mt Koya have histories that stretch back hundreds of years.

From the standpoint of the temples, running accommodation requires staff, food, maintenance and other expenses, and they are operating in a tourism market where visitors are increasingly willing to pay for a more comfortable and exclusive experience. At the same time, these are still religious sites, and the more they resemble luxury hotels and charge luxury prices, the more questions are raised about where the line should be drawn between providing a sustainable service and commercialising a sacred space.

However, the rising prices have not gone over well with a lot of tourists, with Japanese visitors also asking the question: “Are temples supposed to be profit-seeking?”

It’s a tough balance to strike between providing a religious service and earning money to keep old traditions alive. But with the weak yen making experiences that are expensive by Japanese standards seem incredibly cheap to overseas tourists, price increases in the tourist sector are now becoming increasingly common.

Whether these increases are justified or not is up for debate, but when one of the country’s most famous temple communities is involved, there needs to be extra transparency in income reporting and careful thought given to how much is too much when charging for overnight stays.

Sources: Yomiuri Shimbun, Sankei via Yahoo! Japan News

title: Visiting Kagawa’s popular cooking class where you make noodles with your feet
description: Rock out as you dance your way to handmade sanuki udon. Having a meal out is a great experience now and again, but cooking for yourself not only allows you to customize your meal to your liking, it also provides you with a warming sense of accomplishment. However, having a professional by your side to […]
content:
Rock out as you dance your way to handmade sanuki udon.

Having a meal out is a great experience now and again, but cooking for yourself not only allows you to customize your meal to your liking, it also provides you with a warming sense of accomplishment. However, having a professional by your side to gently guide you along the steps to making a famous local food is on a level of its own—particularly when it involves dancing on top of your dough.

▼ Don’t worry, it doesn’t smell like feet.

Kagawa, located on Shikoku, the smallest of Japan’s four main islands, is not one of the nation’s main tourist hubs, and even our Japanese-language reporter Kouhey has only been there a scant two times in the past. It is a well-known home to sanuki udon noodles, which are thick, chewy, and have been proven to calm crying babies, and yet Kouhey has hardly ever eaten the food in this land of noodles, so for his most recent trip there, he sought to remedy this travesty.

The town of Kotohira is a popular tourist destination within Kagawa, famous for Kotohira Shrine (affectionately known as Kompirasan) and its climb with over 700 steps. At the foot of the shrine is Nakano Udon School, a company that is over a century old and has been offering sanuki udon experiences for tourists for over 40 years. It also featured in the post credits scene of Episode 452 of Detective Conan, “The Phantom of Konpira.” Surely such a well-established company would be able to show Kouhey the way to the most delicious noodles.

Of course, being a person with strong impulsive tendencies, Kouhey hadn’t actually planned on delving into the kitchen himself, but he figured “why not?” and waltzed up to the door where the class schedule for the day was posted. There were three columns for the three different classrooms in Building A, Building B, and the West Building. On the day that he was there, only the column for Building B had time plates hung up for 9:30 a.m. and 1:00 p.m., indicating available classes on that day.

Going up to the reception to ask, Kouhey was told the class would take about 50 minutes, and he was in luck as there happened to still be space available to participate. The staff also mentioned that on some days the classes get completely booked, so if you want to make sure you get to experience it, booking in advance on the website is the way to go.

If you participate alone and take the noodles home, like Kouhey, it costs 1,980 yen (US$13), but if you eat them on-site, it’s 2,530 yen. For groups of up to 14 people, it’s 1,760 yen per person, and for 15 or more, it’s 1,650 yen, so be sure to drag all of your friends along for an experience you’re unlikely to forget. Note that for groups, the price doesn’t change whether you take them home or eat them on the spot, so it’s pretty reasonable.

After registering, Kouhey was given the option of what souvenir to take home: a Secret Recipe Scroll that doubles as a rolling pin, or two servings of udon. Without much hesitation, he opted for the scroll.

▼ We’d show you the inside, but… it’s a secret.

As he turned around to wait for the time of the class to start, Kouhey spotted the Nakano Udon School Graduate Signatures from celebrities hanging on the wall, remarking how school-like it felt to have them be called “graduates”.

When he finally entered the venue, Kouhey came to find that the class would be held in a school classroom-esque setting.

Looking around, there were over 20 people, including families with children, with almost all of the seats filled. A male instructor with a dark blue hand towel wrapped around his head stood in front holding a microphone when…

♪~Ding Dong Dang Dong~♪

…Japan’s iconic school chime rang out, and the class began.

First up, Kouhey was handed a lump of dough shaped like a rectangle with rounded corners, which he needed to roll out.

Roll it out, wind it around the rolling pin, and roll it out again.

After that, Kouhey just had to cut it with a knife.

Looking at his completed work closer, Kouhey spotted thick and thin cuts of different sizes, but overall he was pretty pleased with how his first-ever noodles came out.

These noodles could either be boiled and eaten in the cafeteria on the floor below after the class ended, or taken home to cook, which was what Kouhey had chosen to do.

Now, it was time for the main event: making the dough from scratch. First was the process of mixing flour with salted water. The flour goes into the kneading bowl (called a “konebachi”) and the salted water is added from the red cup.

Stirring with fingers held upright, the flour gradually turns into a crumbly texture.

Put this into a plastic bag and flatten it out. Next up was “foot-kneading”.

Place the dough inside a bag on top of a tatami mat, and step on it with just your socks on. While a novel experience, it’s made countless times more fun thanks to the upbeat background music played in the classroom for this part of the lesson, causing you to dance on top of your dough.

It’s hard to tell only by looking at Kouhey’s feet, but dough was being stomped on everywhere around him while the other students also danced along to exciting tracks, bringing out the inner kids in all of the adults. Back in 2016, when I visited the school myself, I rocked out to Gangnam Style and PPAP, with my fellow “classmates” playing the tambourines—ten out of ten, the most fun cooking experience I’ve had to date.

Fold the flattened dough into layers, form it into a rough baumkuchen/roll cake shape, where it will then enter the aging process, which can vary depending on the season. This brings the class to a close.

Under the graduation commemoration sign at the back of the classroom, families and groups of friends lined up to take their photos.

After returning home, Kouhey finally had a chance to compare and eat the udon he had bought at the Nakano Udon School gift shop against the noodles he had rolled and cut himself.

▼ Kouhey’s noodles are on the right.

The moment Kouhey boiled them and arranged them on a plate, they were already clearly different. The noodles from the gift shop had a round cross-section and were neatly uniform in thickness. On the other hand, his noodles were flat, wide, and uneven in thickness.

He had lost in terms of appearance, but it being his first time trying to cut noodles, he had kind of been expecting it.

As for the taste, the gift shop noodles were naturally chewy and delicious.

In contrast, Kouhey’s noodles were missing that ideal firm-on-the-outside, chewy-on-the-inside texture, perhaps because he boiled them too long.

Even so, the emotional impact of eating his own noodles was exceptional. Kouhey may eat oodles of noodles in the future, but he has a newfound respect for the time and effort used to make such delicious food from nothing more than flour, salt, and water, all thanks to this single class he attended. If ever you are in the area, making your own noodles is an experience that you shouldn’t pass on by.

Location information
Nakano Udon Gakko Kotohira-ko / 中野うどん学校 琴平校
Address: Kagawa-ken, Nakatada-gun, Kotohira-cho 796
香川県仲多度郡琴平町796番地
Open 9:00 a.m.–5:30 p.m. (Building A), 9:30 a.m.–4:30 p.m. (Building B)
Udon school operating hours are 9:00 a.m.–3:00 p.m.

title: Pokémon Adidas crossover sneaker line releases in Japan, gives your feet Pikachu hugs [Pics]
description: Collaboration gets off to an early start in Pokémon’s home country. There’s a lot of walking in Pokémon. The young Trainers who serve as the protagonists of the video games and anime are generally too young to drive, and besides, catching ‘em all involves venturing far afield in order to find the rarest Pocket Monster […]
content:
Collaboration gets off to an early start in Pokémon’s home country.

There’s a lot of walking in Pokémon. The young Trainers who serve as the protagonists of the video games and anime are generally too young to drive, and besides, catching ‘em all involves venturing far afield in order to find the rarest Pocket Monster breeds.

So if you’ve got some real-world walking of your own to do, Adidas wants to let you do it in Pokémon sneakers.

The Pokémon 30th Anniversary Adidas Originals line is now on sale in Japan, with the crossover combining some of the most iconic Pokémon with some of Adidas most popular footwear models. Pikachu, naturally, shows up multiple times, first in the Superstar II mid-tops above, with a textured Pikachu hugging your ankles. Meanwhile, the low-top Pikachu Superstar II focuses on the face of the franchise’s ears, while also recreating his fluffy fur on the shoes’ outside.

Two different smile-inducing smiling Pikachus can be found around back, but if you want even more of them walking with you, these will do the trick.

The colors of the Charmander Superstar II will immediately evoke happy memories of time spent with the Gen-I starter…

…and the flames on the side will remind even newer fans know that this is a Fire-type.

Speaking of Charmander, Adidas’ Pokémon collection marks a rare occasion for Charmeleon, Charmander’s first evolution (i.e. his form before evolving into Charizard) to enjoy some time in the spotlight with its own Superstar II version.

Ghost-type fashion comes in the form of a menacing Gengar Adistar XLG 2.0…

…and Haunter Adistar Control 5, which has a more subtle nod to its inspiration in the shape of the shoe’s tongue.

Rayquaza shows up twice, befitting its importance as a Legendary Pokémon, with both Megaride and ZX 500 RS versions…

…or, if you want to show off a real old-school Legendary Pokémon, there’s the Mewtwo Samba OG

Adidas tends to put aesthetics before affordability in its limited-edition models, and the shoes shown above range in price from 16,500 to 33,000 yen (approximately US$105-US$210). They’re available as of September 15 in Japan through the Adidas Japan online shop and Rakuten (here and here), and are scheduled to start making their way to overseas retailers starting September 22.

Source: PR Times, Rakuten

title: Starbucks and clothing brand Beams team up for launch of second collaborative core collection
description: You can wear your love for coffee on your sleeve in this new series of Starbucks Stand by Beams clothing and lifestyle goods–literally, in one case. It’s been a year since Starbucks Japan teamed up with Japanese clothing brand Beams for a joint “Starbucks Stand by Beams” collaboration. Following the success of that first series […]
content:
You can wear your love for coffee on your sleeve in this new series of Starbucks Stand by Beams clothing and lifestyle goods–literally, in one case.

It’s been a year since Starbucks Japan teamed up with Japanese clothing brand Beams for a joint “Starbucks Stand by Beams” collaboration. Following the success of that first series of items that blended fashion and coffee culture, the giants are now gearing up to release a second series in the core collection.

▼ Starbucks Stand by Beams is not even the first time that the two major brands have teamed up for apparel.

The new line will debut on September 18 with 14 types of items, with one each sold exclusively at the Starbucks online shop and Beams stores respectively. All clothing items are unisex and come in sizes extra-small through extra-large, though the Starbucks online shop carries sizes small through extra-large only.

● Logo ringer t-shirts (9,350 yen [US$61])

This timeless design comes in either beige or blue colors with darker accents along the neckline and sleeve hemlines. It’s a made of a rayon blend of heathered fabric.

● Logo zipper hoodies (19,800 yen)

A USA cotton fleece lining lends the ultimate comfort to these brown, green, oatmeal-colored full-zip hoodies.

 

● Logo sweatpants (16,500 yen)

With the same colors to match the above hoodies, these wide sweatpants feature a heavyweight USA cotton fleece lining. They also include a length adjuster and a zippered back pocket.

● Oxford shirt (15,400 yen, exclusive to the Starbucks online shop)

A cute tumbler embroidery graces the front left pocket of this wide-fit Oxford shirt made of heavyweight cotton.

   

● Flap chino pants (19,800 yen, exclusive to Beams stores)

Dress up or dress down in these classically comfortable olive, beige, or brown chino pants that come with flap pockets and adjustable hems.

● Black denim jacket (41,800 yen)

Made with denim from Japan’s leading denim-producing area, Okayama, the jacket’s initial color is faded then subsequently washed using discarded coffee bean husks for a dark, natural coffee hue (there’s no word yet on whether it’s coffee-scented as well).

● Natural color logo PVC pouch (3,960 yen)

This multiuse pouch features different logos on each side, including the familiar Starbucks siren. Its PVC material is water and stain-resistant.

● Clear color logo PVC pouch (3,300 yen)

This one is another multiuse pouch but this time transparent for you to be able to see what’s stored inside.

● Craft paper cool bag (7,150 yen)

Made from Tyvek material, this lunch bag resembles the paper bags given with Starbucks food orders. Built-in aluminum-coated insulation keeps the food inside cool and mesh pockets help you keep things separated.

● Synthetic leather drawstring bag (12,100 yen)

On the slightly more stylish end, this black drawstring bag has two-way functionality with its removable shoulder strap.

● Logo PVC shoulder tote bag (8,800 yen)

Meanwhile, this small tote is perfect for everyday use and is equipped with an interior pocket and carabiner for extra security.

● Coffee cherry bandana (2,970 yen)

These brown and navy-colored bandanas can serve a variety of practical or aesthetic purposes with their intricate design of coffee berries (commonly called “coffee cherries”), leaves, and flowers in a lacelike pattern.

● Drink-ID socks (3,300 yen)

White-and-black socks with the drink customization chart found on the back of Starbucks cups are perfect for that person who customizes every part of their drink. They come in two sizes–small (23-25 centimeters [9-9.8 inches]) and medium (25-27 centimeters).

● To-go bottles (5,800 yen)

The last new item in the core collection is a beige or navy stainless steel bottle designed to capture the look of Starbucks’ paper cups. It has double-layered vacuum insulation, a locking lid, and stores 473 milliliters (16 fluid ounces) of liquid.

 

The Starbucks Stand by Beams collection will be available starting September 18 appear at the Beams Life store in Yokohama, Beams Japan store in Tokyo’s Shinjuku district, and the new Beams Umeda tore in Osaka, as well as at a pop-up store that runs until September 27 at Nagoya Station.

We look forward to seeing what other kinds of creative collaborations Beams takes on next!

title: Ghibli/Kyoto crossover artwork decorates goshuin papers for Zen and Ghibli art exhibition [Pics]
description: Kyoto museum’s ”Ghibli for grown-ups” event collaborates with three Kyoto Zen temples. Temple architecture and anime artwork are both undeniable expressions of Japanese aesthetic sensibilities. Many would say that some of the finest examples of the former can be found in Kyoto, and the latter within the films of Studio Ghibli, and this fall JR […]
content:
Kyoto museum’s ”Ghibli for grown-ups” event collaborates with three Kyoto Zen temples.

Temple architecture and anime artwork are both undeniable expressions of Japanese aesthetic sensibilities. Many would say that some of the finest examples of the former can be found in Kyoto, and the latter within the films of Studio Ghibli, and this fall JR Central is offering something special for fans who enjoy both.

The Kyoto City Kyocera Museum of Art is getting ready to open its Zen and Ghibli exhibition in October. This first-of-its-kind event is “an immersive exhibition exploring Zen through the works of Studio Ghibli,” drawing from a book of the same title written by veteran Ghibli producer Toshio Suzuki. The museum says that “Ghibli films often embody a worldview that does not divide good and evil, leaves space instead of rushing to answers, and embraces the attitude of ‘accepting without fully understanding.’ This resonates deeply with the Zen principles of ‘not dividing,’ ‘not judging,’ and ‘seeing things as they are,’” and the exhibit is structured around The Boy and the Heron, arguably Ghibli’s most open-to-interpretation anime ever, in particular.

▼　The poster for Zen and Ghibli, which the museum is also promoting as “Ghibli-for grown-ups,” features a line of The Boy and the Heron’ s floating warara creatures.

At-the-door admission is 1,900 yen (US$12), but getting your ticket in advance via JR Central’s EX ticketing service will save you 300 yen if you book by October 2, and it’ll still save you 100 yen after that date. More importantly, though, booking through EX will get you some beautiful Ghibli/Kyoto collaborative artwork in the form of goshuin papers.

Goshuin are stamped certificates provided at temples in Japan, certifying the bearer’s visit and said to bestow blessings upon them. They also look really cool, and many travelers enjoy them as a culturally artistic way of commemorating that part of their journey. In the most basic arrangement, the goshuin is transferred onto plain white paper, but the JR Central-reserved Zen and Ghibli ticket includes Ghibli-themed goshuin papers to be used at three famous Kyoto temples. Pictured above is the paper to be used at Shokokuji Temple, with Totoro flying above the temple’s main hall, and there are also papers for Nanzenji and Myoshinji Temples.

▼ The Nanzenji paper features Porco Rosso protagonist Porco.

▼ The Myoshinji paper has who appears to be Howl’s Moving Castle’s Howl in his avian form, but with a bit of a simian touch.

▼ Maybe it’s meant as a nod to “Withered Trees and Monkeys,” a famous work by 16th/17th-century painter Hasegawa Tohaku which has been in Myoshinji’s collection of artwork.

The goshuin papers start off with their left halves blank, as the stamps are to be added upon visiting the respective temples. Alternatively, if you’re a hybrid Ghilbi/goshuin enthusiast who wants something more substantial to be stamped, JR Central is also offering a package with a Zen and Ghibli admission ticket and a goshuin book, with multiple blank pages inside, a front cover illustrated with the adorable warawara, and Princess Mononoke’s San on the back.

Note that while admission to the Zen and Ghibli exhibit is included in the JR Central packages, admission to the three associated temples is separate, as are the fees for the goshuin stamp to be applied.

The packages can be reserved now through the EX website here, with the museum ticket/goshuin papers set 1,600 yen and the ticket/goshuin book bundle 3,300 yen until October 2, and the prices for both going up by 200 yen after that. Zen and Ghibli is scheduled to run from October 3 to December 6, but the goshuin papers/book can be used after the exhibition closes as well.

Source: PR Times (1, 2), Kyoto City Kyosera Museum of Art, Zen and Ghibli official website

title: Japan’s new delicious dark horse sweet potato dessert drink is waiting at a beef bowl chain
description: A beniharuka shake rolls into Sukiya as sweet potato season gets underway. Japan never met a seasonal sweets flavor it couldn’t find space in its heart for, and with sweet potato season here, it’s an especially sweet time of year. The flavor of sweet potatoes is so loved in Japan that there’s even a whole […]
content:
A beniharuka shake rolls into Sukiya as sweet potato season gets underway.

Japan never met a seasonal sweets flavor it couldn’t find space in its heart for, and with sweet potato season here, it’s an especially sweet time of year. The flavor of sweet potatoes is so loved in Japan that there’s even a whole sub-category of sweet potato dessert drinks that arrives every autumn, such as Starbucks Japan’s sweet potato Frappuccino.

But cafes and coffeehouses don’t have a monopoly on drinkable sweet potato treats, and one of the best we’ve had so far this year is at none other than one of Japan’s biggest beef bowl chains.

Along with Yoshinoya and Matsuya, Sukiya is one of Japan’s big three gyudon (beef bowl) restaurants, and their take on the dish has a subtle hint of refreshing citrus to the broth the meat is simmered in.

But Sukiya is ready to satisfy not just carnivorous cravings, as they’ve also got a selection of desserts that they collectively call the “Suki Cafe” line, which includes their Suki Shakes, and as of September 8 they’re serving up sweet potato shakes!

If you’re ordering in Japanese, the flavor is called yakiimo, which translates literally as “roasted potato” but is always used to refer specifically to roasted sweet potatoes. Suki Shakes are generally a vanilla base with another flavor mixed in for an enticing marbled appearance, and in this case the special guest is a sweet potato sauce made with beniharuka grown in Ibaraki Prefecture. Beniharuka are Japan’s sweetest variety of sweet potato, so we had high expectations as we took a sip.

The first thing to register on our taste buds was the milky sweetness of the vanilla portion, which is so creamy that it reminded us of soft-serve ice cream. After that came the sweet potato sauce, which not only tasted delicious but had a stickiness to it, evoking thoughts of the caramelized sugar that seeps out of sweet potatoes during roasting. It was a fantastic combination, and with the crushed pieces of imo kenpi (crisp candied sweet potato chips) sprinkled across the top, you also get some stimulating crunchiness.

Our taste tester Yayoi Saginomiya was so impressed that she’s ready to call this a dark horse contender for the best sweet potato drink you can find this season. In addition to being a far, far more delicious dessert than most people would expect of a beef bowl restaurant, it’s a very affordable one too, costing just 210 yen (US$1.30) for a small size, 260 for a medium, and 350 for a large, so stomach capacity, not budget concerns, is going to be the only limiting factor as to how many of these we can drink during the limited time they’ll be on sale.

title: Making the latest social media snack sensation in Japan, Dot Butter
description: High in both cuteness and calories. The advent of the Internet enabled sharing of strange ways to eat food to a degree never before seen in human history. Whether it’s putting pudding in ramen, eating ramen in a bathtub, or adding sake to ramen, there’s no shortage of ideas that make you wonder both why […]
content:
High in both cuteness and calories.

The advent of the Internet enabled sharing of strange ways to eat food to a degree never before seen in human history. Whether it’s putting pudding in ramen, eating ramen in a bathtub, or adding sake to ramen, there’s no shortage of ideas that make you wonder both why they thought of such a thing and why you never thought of such a thing.

The latest such creation is going by the name of “Dot Butter” on social media. It’s both incredibly simple and unheard of at the same time, simply consisting of a piece of butter with sprinkles. I personally have never felt the urge to eat a spoonful of butter, and I’m not sure sprinkles would sweeten the deal all that much, but one look was enough to give our writer Mai Tsubomi the urge to try some Dot Butter for herself.

She headed to her local supermarket and came home with a pack of sprinkles and some butter. Mai figured the type of butter sold in pre-cut and individually wrapped squares would work well for this particular snack.

Making Dot Butter is extremely simple. Just coat the piece of butter in sprinkles and eat. However, after plopping in her pre-cut butter, Mai noticed a problem.

The piece of butter was a little too small compared to the size of the sprinkles. Because of this, the sprinkles wouldn’t stick everywhere on the butter, leaving bare patches here and there. It turned out that this recipe wasn’t quite as easy as it seems.

It didn’t quite have the visual impact she was hoping for and still felt like she was about to bite into a chunk of butter. Our writer initially panicked, thinking she somehow managed to screw up one of the easiest recipes around. However, once she tasted it, she was pleasantly surprised. The saltiness of the butter mingled well with the sweetness of the sprinkles.

Luckily, Mai’s first experience with Dot Butter was a good one, but she still felt like it could have been better. So she went to the kitchen, got a stick of regular butter, and cut off a piece large enough to fully accept the sprinkles while also keeping her own health in mind as one should when eating pure butter.

It looked much better and tasted just as good at first, but a few more bites in and she began to notice an oily film form in her mouth. It became too much to bear, and she decided to spread the remainder on some toast instead. Clearly, balance was the key in creating Dot Butter that’s both good-looking and pleasant to eat.

With this new taste sensation under her belt, Mai started to wonder what if more commonly edible dairy squares were used in the place of butter. So she also prepared the ingredients to make Dot Cream Cheese and Dot Mozzarella.

Fortunately for our writer, both came out surprisingly good. In fact, she’d say they were both better than Dot Butter. The Dot Cream Cheese was the better of the two, with a delicious tang and the feeling of eating some cheesecake. Dot Mozzarella, on the other hand, had the same delectable balance of sweet and salty that the butter had, but without the greasy mouthfeel.

She still felt Dot Butter itself is a really nice treat when done in moderation and had a certain forbidden charm that the other squares were somewhat lacking in. One thing to point out is that most sprinkles in Japan are made from chocolate, and results may vary when using sugar-based sprinkles, though I can’t imagine how. So go ahead and add a little color to your life from time to time.
